Residential Zoned Land Tax (RZLT)
The Residential Zoned Land Tax Final Map for 2026 was published 
on 31st January 2026 and shows lands subject to the tax. The 
RZLT annual review process commenced on 1st February 2026 
with the publication of the Annual Draft Map for 2027.
The purpose of the RZLT is to activate land that is zoned and 
serviced for residential or mixed use to increase housing supply 
and to ensure the regeneration of vacant and idle lands in urban 
locations. Local authorities are responsible for the preparation of 
mapping identifying lands considered ‘in scope’ and the Revenue 
Commissioners are responsible for the collection of the tax. RZLT 
is an annual tax charged at 3% of the market value of ‘in scope’ 
lands. 
There is an opportunity to make submissions on both maps until 
1st April 2026. In relation to the RZLT Final Map 2026, landowners 
may request the local authority to change the zoning status of 
land included on the map. In relation to the RZLT Annual Draft 
Map 2027 landowners and members of the public can make 
submissions regarding the inclusion or exclusion of lands to the 
RZLT map.
Both RZLT maps are published on the Clare County Council 
website, at https://www.clarecoco.ie/planning-and-building/
residential-zoned-land-tax-rzlt/residential-zoned-land-tax-
rzlt, along with information on the RZLT and how to make a 
submission. Maps are also available for members of the public to 
view at Council offices around the county.

Under the revised approach, anyone fleeing the war in Ukraine,

arrive. 
This change will not affect people who have already commenced 
their stay under the 90-day Accommodation Policy, or those 
already availing of other State-supported accommodation.
LOCAL AUTHORITY INTEGRATION 
TEAM 
 
The Local Authority Integration Teams (LAITs) have been set up 
in all local authorities. Their purpose is to help coordinate the 
different kinds of support available for people who are applying 
for international protection, refugees, and others in similar 
situations.   
The goal of LAITs is to help IP applicants and refugees become 
independent, settle into their new communities, and participate 
in Irish life. They do this by connecting people to important 
services that can help them integrate into the community.   
Who do LAITs support? 
LAITs provide support for: 
•	
Applicants for International Protection (IP) 
•	
People who have been granted refugee status or other forms 
of protection, such as subsidiary protection or permission to 
remain 
•	
Refugees who have been resettled in Ireland through a 
government programme 
•	
Beneficiaries of Temporary Protection (BOTPs) 
How is the support provided? 
LAITs operate under the principle of 'Integration from Day One'. 
This means that LAITs provide integration support to people who 
need it as soon as they arrive in Ireland. 
What services do LAITs provide? 
The work of LAITs isn’t meant to replace existing services. Instead, 
LAITs help connect people with the existing services that are most 
suitable for their needs. This includes things like: 
•	
Being a direct contact for new arrivals, helping them with any 
problems they might have when dealing with public services 
•	
Connecting new arrivals with services like legal help, 
childcare and healthcare 
•	
Connecting new arrivals with services that improve their 
ability to live independently, like job training, English classes, 
education, and apprenticeships 
•	
Guiding new arrivals through the process of applying for 
financial support, medical help, child benefits, and other 
services they might need 
•	
Holding meetings in local areas and using community 
development principles to help those who attend 
•	
Supporting people if they face racism or other unfair 
treatment, helping them report it to the right authorities 
•	
Helping vulnerable new arrivals get in touch with non-

Ryan was appointed Chairperson and Cllr Rita McInerney 
was appointed Vice Chairperson. The Terms of Reference and 
Standing Orders were adopted by consensus, and a Working

Local Community Safety Plan.

October 2025. The revised structure includes a dedicated Housing

The HAU has been in regular contact with the Housing Activation 
Officer within DHLGH regarding infrastructure projects required 
to unlock housing delivery. The Housing Activation Office has 
responsibility for the Housing Infrastructure Investment Fund 
(HIIF) which was launched in January 2026.

Ireland for many years and forms part of a broader suite of 
land activation measures included in the plan to support the 
Government’s target to construct 300,000 homes by the end of 
2030. The HIIF will support direct investment in infrastructure 
needed to unlock the development of housing in towns and 
cities nationwide. The key criteria for a project submitted for 
consideration for HIIF funding are that that the project:
•	
Is public infrastructure;
•	
Enables the delivery of new homes; and 
•	
Is substantially completed by 2028.

deadline for submissions to Call 1 is Friday 27 February 2026.

This unit operates within the Housing Delivery, Infrastructure 
Provision and Land Activation Directorate and the key objective 
being to bring together our resources with a strong ambition for 
delivery of increased activation of vacant and derelict properties 
throughout the County. The Property Management unit deals 
with the Council owned lands and properties.
Working collaboratively across the other units in the Directorate 
with pooled resources and knowledge, it is intended to increase 
levels of activity and engagement to activate more properties for 
delivery of housing, both public and private.
Taking action on dereliction and vacancy is a priority in the 
National Housing Plan 2025, with the re-use and regeneration 
of vacant and derelict properties in cities, towns and villages 
providing much needed housing and transforming and revitalizing 
communities, as summarised hereunder.
 
DERELICT SITES
In recent months, the Minister for Housing has clearly prioritised 
action on Dereliction, telling property owners that: “under my 
watch, there will be nowhere for them to hide". In line with this 
direction, the Council is now increasing the number of properties 
being inspected, notices being served on owners, derelict sites 
levies being billed and in particular the number of properties 
being identified for compulsory acquisition under the Derelict 
Sites legislation. 
A significant effort to transform derelict properties across the 
County is underway with 350 derelict properties being 
dealt with by the Derelict Sites Team as of the 24th February 
2026. A further 30 properties have been identified for action 
in the last month. The team maintains very high levels of 
activity and engagement with owners and their legal/technical 
representatives. This initial engagement is key to resolution of 
the issues of dereliction and to gain an understanding of the 
various reasons why the properties are in a derelict state. Where 
derelict properties are sold by the owner, the Derelict Sites Team 
engages promptly with the new owners to brief them on their 
responsibilities under the Derelict Sites Act, 1990. 
Turning the Tide on Dereliction
Tackling dereliction and bringing much-needed properties, 
particularly dwellings, back into use requires a lot more than just 
a coat of paint; it demands a concerted drive that leverages the 
full legal weight of the Derelict Sites Act 1990. For too long, these 
derelict buildings have drained the vitality of our communities, 
detracting from the general amenity and character of the area. 
To turn the tide, Derelict Sites Section in Clare County Council is 
implementing an intensified systematic and proactive approach. 
We are increasing the numbers of properties across the county 
that we are pursuing under the legislation i.e. 303 properties at 
end of 2025 compared to 350 at today’s date and making full use 
of the legislative powers available.
To bolster the momentum, the Council is advising property 
owners on accessing the vacant property refurbishment grant. 
The Team is also seeing a consistent number of planning

UNESCO Global Geopark
New Fossil discovery in Burren and Cliffs of Moher UNESCO Global 
Geopark
A 320-million-year-old fossil horseshoe crab that was found near 
the Cliffs of Moher has been described and published in the 
Irish Journal of Earth Sciences. The specimen was found by Dr. 
Pierre Geuriau as part of a long-term collaboration between the 
Geopark Geologist Dr. Eamon Doyle and the Paris Museum of 
Natural History. The specimen has been identified as Euproops 
cf. danae, the first ever record of this fossil from Ireland. It is an 
arthropod, but despite the name, not actually a crab; it is more 
closely related to spiders and scorpions. It is over 100 years since 
the last fossil horseshoe crab was found in Ireland.

The Scariff office, selected as one of two pilot locations, has 
successfully upgraded from an outdated legacy phone system to 
a modern, cloud-based telephone solution. Past reliability issues, 
aggravated by damage from Storm Eowyn, exposed the limitations 
and reliability issues of the legacy solution and highlighted the 
need for an upgrade. Although the supplier worked to keep the 
old solution functioning at an acceptable level, the expense of 
fully repairing the previous infrastructure could not be justifiable.
Following a procurement process, Clare County Council selected 
Procloud Technologies - a leading provider of enterprise 
infrastructure and IP telephony solutions - to partner in deploying, 
evaluating, and supporting the new system.

the Shannon office, with the upgrade expected to be completed 
by early March.

phone features and offers greater flexibility for future 
expansion if needed. It eliminates reliance on legacy and costly 
communication links. Proves enhanced reporting capabilities and 
support for flexible work arrangements allowing staff to make 
and receive calls even when working remotely.
